## Abstract

Many quantum networking applications require efficient photonic interfaces to quantum memories which can be produced at scale and with high yield. Synthetic diamond offers unique potential for the implementation of this technology as it hosts color centers which retain coherent optical interfaces and long spin coherence times in nanophotonic structures. Here, we report a technique enabling wafer-scale processing of thin-film diamond that combines ion implantation and membrane liftoff, high-quality overgrowth, targeted color center implantation, and serial, high-throughput thermocompression bonding with yields approaching unity. The deterministic deposition of thin diamond membranes onto semiconductor substrates facilitates consistent integration of photonic crystal cavities with silicon-vacancy (SiV) quantum memories. We demonstrate reliable, strong coupling of SiVs to photons with cooperativities approaching 100. Furthermore, we show that photonic crystal cavities can be reliably fabricated across several membranes bonded to the same handling chip. Our platform enables modular fabrication where the photonic layer can be integrated with functionalized substrates featuring electronic control lines such as coplanar waveguides for microwave delivery. Finally, we implement passive optical packaging with sub-decibel insertion loss. Together, these advances pave the way to the scalable assembly of optically addressable quantum memory arrays which are a key building block for modular photonic quantum interconnects.

## Introduction

Leveraging wafer-scale fabrication of semiconductor materials has been critical to the rapid improvements of classical computing and telecommunications technologies over the past 40 years. Many quantum technologies ranging from computing to networking to sensing would similarly benefit in both performance and scale from high-quality, high-yield wafer-scale fabrication [1]. One example use-case for wafer-scale fabrication of quantum devices is quantum memories. Memories can be used to connect many individual quantum processing units via interconnect channels utilizing quantum memories as network buffer to compensate for channel losses [2]. The scalability of this approach hinges on the ability to fabricate large numbers of high-quality quantum memories, making solid-state memory approaches of particular interest. However, wafer-scale fabrication approaches are only directly applicable to a relatively small set of materials, preventing many materials hosting some of the most promising quantum memories from being produced at scale in an economically viable manner [3, 4].

Synthetic diamond is one example material which has long been recognized for its unique optical, quantum, and mechanical properties, but cannot be produced at wafer scale with sufficiently low strain and defect density for quantum technology applications. This fabrication bottleneck has slowed the deployment of diamond-based technologies for quantum sensing, computation, and communication, which these unique material properties enable [5].

In particular, diamond is among the leading platforms for the implementation of quantum sensors [6, 7] and the production of efficiently interfaced, heralded quantum memories which are key to practical implementations of quantum networks as they enable repeat-until-success protocols [8, 9]. Optically active spin defects based on group-IV vacancy centers in diamond stand out for combining highly coherent optical interfaces and long spin coherence times [10, 11] with the crucial advantage of inversion symmetry that minimizes spectral diffusion in nanophotonic devices [12]. The performance of a quantum network node depends not only on per-channel storage fidelity, efficiency, and bandwidth, but also on the total number of parallel memory channels [4]. Large-scale production of multi-channel diamond memory devices would mark a key step towards modular architectures for utility-scale quantum computers, and novel applications such as blind quantum computing [13], long-baseline telescopes [14, 15] and distributed sensing [16, 17].

Fabrication of high-quality diamond photonic devices has long been accomplished using bespoke nanofabrication techniques on small, standalone bulk diamond dies which limits the yield and scale of the produced technologies. An angled-etching technique [18, 19, 20] has been used to carve out devices from electronic grade bulk diamond, enabling proof-of-concept demonstrations of a variety of quantum optic and nanomechanical implementations. Unfortunately, these bulk-carving techniques are incompatible with foundry manufacturing of photonic integrated circuits. Quasi-isotropic diamond undercutting [21, 22, 23, 24, 25] has also been used to produce individual high-quality devices, but scaling this approach remains challenging due to roughness-limited quality factors and strong crystallographic and aspect ratio dependent etch behavior.

Here, we demonstrate a major advancement towards large-scale production of quantum memories with a deterministic, highly efficient optical interface, and heterogeneous integration to substrates functionalized with electronic control lines (Fig. 1). Our approach involves high-yield deposition and parallelized patterning of a matrix of diamond thin films on a wafer featuring several pre-patterned individual dies. This technology represents a critical step towards scalable fabrication of hundreds of diamond devices in a single fabrication run on wafer-scale substrates without requiring access to wafer-scale quantum-grade diamond.

Our platform utilizes homogeneous, single-crystalline diamond films created by combining an ion implantation and liftoff technique with high-purity diamond overgrowth [26, 27]. Such thin-film diamonds have been shown to be suitable for hosting quantum memories with lifetime-limited optical transitions and long spin coherence times [28]. Additionally, key quantum memory components including photonic interfaces, such as photonic crystal cavities [29] and slow-light waveguides [30], as well as spin control [31] have been demonstrated in individual diamond films.

To demonstrate the large-scale fabrication capabilities enabled by our diamond films, we develop a robust fabrication pipeline for high-quality devices with close-to-unity yield. We report significant progress along several axes including high-quality, high-uniformity diamond overgrowth, deterministic implantation of color centers through nanoapertures, parallelized electrochemical etching and single-step millimeter-scale membrane deposition achieved via metal thermocompression bonding with near-unity yield. We demonstrate the deposition of tens of membranes to the same handling chip which can be extended to full wafer reconstitution where many individual membranes are tiled to cover the wafer surface for further processing.

High-cooperativity interfaces for deterministic silicon-vacancy (SiV) memory-photon interactions can be implemented routinely on this platform. We demonstrate that we can fabricate photonic crystal cavities reliably and in parallel for several membranes bonded to the same handling chip with small spread in resonance wavelength while maintaining high quality factors.

Our process is streamlined by separating fabrication of optical components in diamond and functionalizing layers in the substrate. Device applications and performance can be tuned by introducing layers featuring different electronic or photonic components. Importantly, the high temperature processing necessary for creating defect centers is separated from front-end fabrication of electronic or photonic components with lower temperature tolerances (e.g. electronic control lines). Moreover, alignment between the substrate and devices on the film can be accomplished lithographically, eliminating the need for nanometer scale alignment during a pick-and-place integration step [24].

When combined with wafer-scale fabrication, our approach paves the way towards large scale integration of memory-based quantum interconnect nodes with many efficient photonic and electronic channels. Our platform represents a crucial step towards utility-scale quantum computers implemented with efficient interconnection of individual quantum processing units based on ions [32] or atoms [33].

## Results

### High-yield fabrication of high-quality diamond membranes

We implement a high-yield, scalable fabrication pipeline for the generation of high-quality diamond membranes bonded to a semiconductor substrate. Our process combines ion implantation and membrane liftoff, high-purity diamond overgrowth, nanoaperture implantation of quantum memories and flip-chip thermocompression bonding to fabricate diamond membranes and photonic devices with high yield (Fig. 2(a(i-x)), methods).

We report several significant advancements compared to previously reported approaches [26, 27]. First, by masking the edge of the diamond substrate during ion implantation, we retain a solid diamond frame which anchors the membrane during undercutting and bonding (Fig. 2(a,i)). Second, a systematic study of the growth conditions for homoepitaxial high-purity diamond results in consistent creation of diamond layers with low surface roughness ( $<\,0.2\,\text{nm}$ root mean square (RMS)) and thickness variation ( $<$ 20 nm) across the diamond (Fig. 2(a,ii), methods). Finally, targeted ion implantation of SiV color centers through nanoapertures (Fig. 2(a,iii)) significantly increases the final device yield by reducing background fluorescence from unintentionally created, weakly coupled SiV centers.

To prepare an array of diamond membranes bonded to a wafer, we define a tethered array of micromembranes via aligned trench fabrication (Fig. 2(a,iv)) which enables collective undercutting of the whole membrane array simultaneously using electro-chemical etching (Fig. 2(a,v), Fig. 2(b)). We metalize the surface and use aligned flip-chip thermocompression bonding (Fig. 2(a,vi)) to deterministically transfer membranes from the parent diamond to handling chips with high throughput ( $<1\,\text{min}$ per bond) and high yield (Fig. 2(a,vii)). Finally, photonic structures are fabricated by first thinning down the membrane to the desired thickness (Fig. 2(a,viii)), employing standard top-down semiconductor fabrication techniques (Fig. 2(a,ix)) and finally undercutting the structures using wet chemical etching (Fig. 2(a,x)).

Our high-throughput transfer process is a key step toward wafer-scale fabrication, enabling the creation of large-scale device arrays by depositing a matrix of many membranes on a single silicon handling chip without replacing the substrate or parent diamond. For this demonstration we define an array of hexagonal membranes with a lateral dimension of 0.5 mm arranged in a honeycomb lattice weakly tethered to a frame. We employ gold thermocompression bonding to form a strong continuous bonding layer to a commensurate gold pad on a Si handling chip. When the parent diamond is retracted, the tethers break off the support frame leaving the membrane bonded. The next membrane is then bonded to the handling chip by moving to and aligning with the next bonding pad (Fig. 2(c)). The bonding process is repeated up to 25 times with a single parent diamond die (Fig. 2(d)). The malleable metal interlayer mitigates the effects of particle contamination and surface irregularities, such as hillocks or pits, that can form during overgrowth. Figure 2(e) displays a $3\times 6$ grid of membranes spaced by 5 mm which were deposited consecutively showcasing the near-unity yield of our process.

### Implementation of high-cooperativity interface to quantum memories

Following membrane bonding to substrate, we create a deterministic, low-background photonic interface for diamond quantum memories by precisely aligning the fabrication of photonic crystal cavities with implanted color centers. After bonding, membranes are thinned to a thickness of 160 nm resulting in a low surface roughness of less than $0.3\,\text{nm}$ RMS. We then fabricate a $4\times 32$ array of photonic crystal cavities using standard top-down fabrication methods (Fig. 2(f), methods).

Our devices implement high-cooperativity interfaces for controlling SiV color centers in diamond, showcasing the excellent quality of our material. For characterization we measure the cavity reflection spectra using a movable tapered fiber probe in a dilution refrigerator with a base temperature of 20 mK (Fig. 3(a)). We deposit nitrogen ice on the devices to red shift the cavity resonances and subsequently use a laser for controlled nitrogen sublimation to tune the cavities into resonance with embedded SiV centers [34]. Scanning a narrow-linewidth laser we resolve sharp spectral features that reveal SiV centers which are well-coupled to the cavity mode (Fig. 3(b)). By fitting the modulation of the cavity reflection spectrum [2], we extract a cavity cooperativity $C=4g^{2}/(\kappa_{\text{tot}}\cdot\gamma_{\text{SiV}})=92$ . The SiV center at $f_{\text{SiV}}=406.74\,\text{THz}$ is assumed to have a lifetime-limited linewidth $\gamma_{\text{SiV}}=94\,\text{MHz}$ , while the cavity has total linewidth of $\kappa_{\text{tot}}=5.73\,\text{GHz}$ . The atom-photon coupling strength is fitted to be $g=3.52\,\text{GHz}$ .

Figure 3(c) shows the distribution of cooperativities of devices which we pre-select via confocal PL measurements in a 4 K cryostat across 3 different chips. Of the 12 devices measured, 9 featured SiV centers coupled with cooperativities $C>5$ , demonstrating that we can deterministically create efficient spin-photon interfaces for which the off-resonant cavity reflection is high and the reflection contrast between spin states is large and robust against spectral diffusion.

Next, we apply an external magnetic field along the SiV axis to lift the degeneracy of the SiV spin states (see level scheme in Fig. 3(a)). The exact alignment of the magnetic field will determine the excited state decay branching ratio of SiV into the spin states. Due to different g-factors in the ground and excited states, the optical transitions for different spin states are at different frequencies, resulting in spin-state-dependent cavity reflection (Fig. 3(d)). Locking the laser to the point of maximum reflection contrast between the two spin states, we observe quantum jumps from which we infer a spin-relaxation time of $T_{1}=32\,\text{s}$ under weak illumination setting a lower bound for the actual $T_{1}$ time (Fig. 3(e)).

### Parallel fabrication of photonic devices

*Figure 4: (a) Bonding of 4 diamond membranes on the same handling chip spaced by 15 mm for parallel fabrication of arrays of thin-film devices; Zoom on membranes after fabrication of a $4\times 32$ array of photonic crystal cavities; Representative cavity reflection scan yielding a quality factor $Q=3.20\times 10^{4}$ at wavelength $\lambda_{\text{cav}}=743.5\,\text{nm}$ . (b) Histograms of cavity resonance wavelengths and quality factors on the same block of 48 devices across the 4 different membranes.*

To confirm the compatibility of our platform with wafer-scale production, we fabricate parallel arrays ( $4\times 32$ ) of photonic crystal cavities of an identical design on four diamond membranes which were bonded 15 mm apart on a single handling chip (Fig. 4(a)). We measure quality factors and resonance wavelengths to capture differences in device performance introduced by variations in the membranes and the fabrication process. We focus on measuring a subset of 48 devices on every membrane (Fig. 4(a)) to limit the number of required measurements and exclude devices with known proximity effect shifts.

Figure 4(a) displays a reflection measurement for a representative device with quality factor $Q=3.20\times 10^{4}$ at wavelength $\lambda_{\text{cav}}=743.5\,\text{nm}$ which is close to being critically coupled with a contrast of $92.5\%$ . We determine quality factors and resonance wavelengths of our devices at room temperature by coupling a supercontinuum laser into the diamond waveguide through a tapered optical fiber interface and record a broadband reflection spectrum using a spectrometer.

We confirm the high quality of our devices and reproducibility of the fabrication by demonstrating average quality factors exceeding $2\times 10^{4}$ with a small spread of resonance wavelengths $<2\,\text{nm}$ across all fabricated membranes (Fig. 4(b)). We find wavelength distributions of $(744.7\pm 1.9)\,\text{nm}$ , $(744.2\pm 1.8)\,\text{nm}$ , $(751.2\pm 1.6)\,\text{nm}$ and $(747.3\pm 1.4)\,\text{nm}$ with corresponding $Q_{\text{tot}}$ factor distributions of $(2.36\pm 0.41)\times 10^{4}$ , $(2.20\pm 0.49)\times 10^{4}$ , $(2.21\pm 0.38)\times 10^{4}$ , $(2.18\pm 0.35)\times 10^{4}$ , respectively. The achieved spread in cavity wavelengths is well within the $\sim 10\,\text{nm}$ cryogenic tuning range afforded by the employed nitrogen gas condensation technique, enabling a near-unity yield of usable, resonant cavities across an entire wafer. This is a significant advancement compared to angled etched devices, where the wavelength spread within one chip is so large that typically only $\sim~10\%$ of fabricated cavities are within the tuning range of optical transition of the SiV center.

We note that global shifts in wavelengths can easily be achieved by adjusting the input design. Run-to-run variations can be compensated by adding witness chips which are readily available due to the high-throughput of our membrane fabrication technique. Variations between membranes can be further improved by adjusting the input design based on metrology steps during fabrication to compensate for thickness variations of the diamond membrane, lithography resist and etching hardmask [35]. Overall, device optimization for diamond photonics based on previous techniques is typically slow or costly since optimization runs either require proxy fabrication tests or a large number of samples. After removing the material bottleneck and paving the way towards wafer-scale fabrication, we anticipate that in dedicated foundry environments the material platform will be improved further and will have close-to-unity yields.

### Integration of membranes with functionalized substrates

We showcase the potential for implementing efficient, fully packaged diamond quantum memories using our fabrication technology by demonstrating integration with functionalized substrates and highly efficient photonic packaging based on our previously demonstrated tapered-fiber technology [36, 37]. We deposit diamond films implanted with nitrogen-vacancy centers onto silicon substrates functionalized with a buried coplanar waveguide (bCPW) for microwave delivery featuring a 1 µm thick silicon dioxide cladding layer (Fig. 5(a,b)). These substrates are fabricated at wafer scale and planarized using chemical mechanical polishing, enabling high-throughput and high-yield production. Diamond films can be bonded onto multiple different coplanar waveguide devices in parallel and then patterned collectively, further improving the rate at which integrated diamond photonic devices, such as sensors, can be produced.

As a proof-of-concept, we drive spin transitions of implanted NV centers (methods) using microwave pulses generated via the bCPW. By adjusting an external magnetic field, we isolate and measure optically detected magnetic resonance of a small ensemble of NV centers with the same orientation (Fig. 5(c)). Coherent spin control is implemented by applying resonant microwave pulses through an integrated coplanar waveguide beneath the diamond membrane (Fig. 5(d)). We measure Rabi oscillations of the NV spin under continuous driving. A microwave power of 15 dBm results in $t_{\pi}=55\,\text{ns}$ . With such microwave field strengths per input power the bCPW should immediately be applicable for the implementation of integrated SiV quantum memory devices. Importantly, the bCPW enables addressing of several devices in parallel by significantly reducing the heat load caused by microwave driving in contrast to patterning the CPW on the diamond surface [38].

Harnessing modular fabrication and the potential for integration of diamond thin films with functionalized substrates constitutes a major step towards practical applications of quantum memories. In previous approaches the fabrication of on-chip CPWs for microwave delivery and spin control required subsequent fabrication steps after the photonics fabrication was complete which increases complexity and reduces device yield. Moreover, aligned lithography and evaporation steps have an inherent risk of damaging devices due to additional handling steps. Furthermore, addressing several devices in parallel is challenging as heat is more difficult to dissipate for metal traces fabricated directly atop a diamond thin film.

To further illustrate the scalability of our approach we demonstrate efficient optical packaging of thin-film devices which enables device operation without any active alignment. Figure 6(a) displays a scanning electron microscope image of a packaged device where the tapered fiber is permanently attached to a photonic crystal device via a tapered waveguide coupler. This fiber attachment method maintains a fiber-to-chip coupling efficiency comparable to that achieved through optimized active alignment techniques. The coupling efficiency of our system is measured to be $\eta_{c}\sim 85\%$ ( $<1\,\text{dB}$ loss) by comparing the cavity reflection with that of a retroreflector. With further optimization, the insertion loss can be reduced to $<0.5\,\text{dB}$ as demonstrated in angled-etched devices [37].

### Discussion and Outlook

This work represents a substantial advance in the scalable fabrication of high-cooperativity quantum devices. The thin-film diamond platform combines high-yield membrane deposition, deterministic color center placement, high-uniformity photonic crystal cavity fabrication, and microwave control. These features have collectively enabled the routine realization of spin-photon interfaces with cooperativities $C>5$ achieved across multiple chips, highlighting the material and process quality. Among these, our best devices achieved very high cooperativities with $C\sim 100$ and are comparable to state-of-the-art implementations across solid-state platforms [2, 39].

We highlight that our ability to fabricate membrane arrays with near-unity yield and the scalable, robust fabrication of photonic crystal cavities with desired properties on several membranes in parallel pave the way to wafer-scale device fabrication. We report high quality factors ( $Q\sim 2\times 10^{4}$ ) across multiple bonded membranes and a narrow spread of cavity resonances within individual membranes ( $<2\,\text{nm}$ ). We anticipate that wavelength shifts between membranes can be eliminated by both adding metrology steps during fabrication and by transferring our process from a shared user facility to a dedicated fabrication facility. The demonstrated yield and uniformity mark a critical leap from earlier bespoke techniques that suffered from limited scalability and reproducibility.

In addition to high-speed microwave control, functionalized substrates will provide multiple electrical signals for the control of SiV quantum memories, for example via strain tuning [40] and could enable more complex complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor circuits for signal processing compatible with cryogenic environments [41]. Our platform enables integration with bCPW structures, as demonstrated by coherent microwave control of NV centers in thin-film diamond. Such integration forms the basis for the large scale production of packaged quantum sensors with low cost, size, weight, and power characteristics [42].

This integration with bCPWs, combined with our previously demonstrated efficient optical fiber packaging, enables fully packaged, electrically and optically addressable quantum memory architectures. The number of optical I/Os, which is limited by the diamond membrane size, can be improved significantly by harnessing heterogeneous optical integration with platforms like lithium niobate or silicon nitride.

The use of metal thermocompression bonding in our current platform offers robust membrane attachment and high-throughput processing. Heterogeneous integration with both photonic and electronic components will be enabled by oxide bonding as demonstrated on bCPW substrates (Fig. 6(b)). This metal-free integration approach shows promise for simplifying downstream processing, improving cleanliness at the bond interface, and expanding material compatibility. We anticipate that in foundry-level fabrication the bonding yield will approach similar levels as with metal thermocompression bonding.

In conclusion, our work constitutes a major step toward wafer-scale, industrial-grade fabrication of integrated quantum memories and sensors. The demonstrated yield, performance, and versatility of our platform represent key enablers for building scalable quantum networks and sensing systems. We anticipate that continued development along the oxide bonding pathway and integration with photonic circuits will position thin-film diamond as a central material in future heterogeneous quantum technologies.

## Methods

### Diamond membrane fabrication

Diamond membranes are fabricated by combining an ion implantation and liftoff technique with high-purity diamond overgrowth. A single-crystal diamond is first polished, and a subsurface graphitized layer is created at a well-defined depth via high-energy helium implantation (0.5 MeV, 7-degree tilt, $5\times 10^{16}\,\text{cm}^{-2})$ . We mask the edge of the diamond during implantation resulting in a solid diamond frame which anchors the membrane during undercutting and bonding. High-temperature annealing ( $1300\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ , $1\times 10^{-6}\,\text{Pa}$ , 120 min) is used to convert this damage layer into graphite. After annealing, fuming H2SO4 + KNO3 is used to remove the graphitization on the surface. Then a high-purity layer of diamond is produced above it via homoepitaxial high-purity overgrowth. This layer is grown to have a typical thickness of $\sim 0.5\,\text{\textmu m}$ with low thickness variation across the diamond (typically $<10\,\text{nm}/1\,\text{mm}$ , Ext. Fig. 1(a)) and low surface roughness ( $<0.2\,\text{nm}$ RMS, Ext. Fig. 1(b)). Alignment marks are fabricated, and SiV color centers are introduced via aligned silicon ion implantation (28Si, 125 kV, $1\times 10^{12}\,\text{cm}^{-2}$ ) through nanoapertures in a PMMA/MMA resist stack and subsequent high-temperature annealing ( $1250\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ , $1\times 10^{-8}\,\text{Pa}$ , 90 min) enabling aligned integration with photonic devices. We then lithographically pattern trenches into diamond to define a tethered array of micromembranes. Finally, we undercut the membranes using electro-chemical etching [43]. We define bonding pads on silicon substrates with respective sizes corresponding to the diamond micromembranes dimensions using optical lithography. We then deposit bonding material on both the surface of the diamond and the bonding pads utilizing either 50 nm titanium and 100 nm gold or silicon dioxide. Finally, we employ flip-chip bonding (Finetech Sigma) to deterministically bond the membranes with high yield at low temperature ( $150\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ ), pressure (5 kPa) and bonding time (15 s). We deposit membranes with unity yield and high throughput ( $<1\,\text{min}$ per bond). To achieve the desired thickness suitable for photonic integration (typically between 100–300 nm), the substrates were thinned via oxygen-based inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP-RIE).

### Fabrication of nanophotonic cavities

We design single-sided photonic crystal cavities with a quadratically tapered lattice constant. The number of incoupling mirror units was optimized for preferential coupling to the waveguide mode, from which light is extracted using a tapered fiber probe. A silicon nitride (SiN) hard mask is deposited via plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition followed by spin-coating of ZEP520A resist. Photonic crystal cavities are defined by electron beam lithography and subsequently transferred to the SiN layer using inductively-coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP-RIE) with a C4F8/SF6/H2 gas mixture. After removal of the resist, the pattern is transferred into the thin-film diamond using O2-based ICP-RIE. The SiN mask and the underlying metal bonding layer are then removed via immersion in dilute hydrofluoric acid and gold etchant and the devices are uniformly undercut via isotropic etching of the silicon substrate with XeF2

### Fabrication of buried coplanar waveguides

bCPW samples are created on a 4-inch silicon wafer using metal liftoff and oxide deposition. We first pattern coplanar waveguides using photo lithography using a bilayer LOR/S1805 resist stack for liftoff and deposit 100 nm gold with 10 nm of chromium as adhesion layer on both sides. Next, we use inductively coupled chemical vapor deposition to deposit $\sim~2\,\text{\textmu m}$ of SiO2 and apply chemical-mechanical polishing to smoothen the surface reducing the thickness to $\sim~1\,\text{\textmu m}$ . NV centers were created in diamond membranes at a depth of $\sim~60\,\text{nm}$ under the surface by implanting nitrogen ions (N+,50 keV, $1\times 10^{12}\,\text{cm}^{-2}$ ) and subsequent high-temperature annealing ( $1250\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ , $10\times 10^{-8}\,\text{Pa}$ , 90 min). The diamond membranes are thinned down to $\sim~300\,\text{nm}$ and the bonding pad is partially undercut by patterning holes into the diamond film to remove the bonding metal layer between membrane and bCPW lines.

### Experimental setup

The experimental setup and methods used for mK nanophotonic cavity quantum electrodynamics experiments involving SiV centers is detailed in a separate publication [44]. All measurements are conducted in a dilution refrigerator (BlueFors BF-LD250) with a base temperature of 20 mK. This refrigerator includes a superconducting vector magnet (American Magnets Inc., 1-1-1 T), a custom-built free-space wide-field microscope with a cryogenic aspherical lens, piezo positioners (Attocube ANPx101 and ANPx311 series), and both fiber and microwave feedthroughs. A gas condensation and laser backtuning technique is used to tune the nanocavity resonance. The SiV-cavity system is addressed optically through a fiber network via a tapered fiber coupler [36, 37], eliminating the need for free-space optics.

Experiments involving the microwave driving of NV centers via buried coplanar waveguides (bCPWs) were performed using a standard confocal microscopy setup. An ensemble of NV centers is optically excited using a green laser diode (Laes Electronics DLNSec 520) and the emission is read out using an avalanche photodiode (Excelitas SPCM 14/16) after being filtered through a 600 nm dichroic and a 670/70 nm bandpass filter. We collect APD counts using a timetagger (Swabian Time Tagger Ultra). In order to generate pulse sequences for microwave driving and gating of excitation/detection, we use a pulsestreamer (Swabian Pulsestreamer 8/2). We use a signal generator (R&S SMB100B) as well as a microwave switch (CMCS0947A-C2) to generate the microwave signals required for ODMR and Rabi measurements.

## Abstract

Distributed quantum computing requires rapid, high-fidelity entanglement between qubits in separate processor modules. Photonic links between single-atom qubits provide switchable, long-range connections, but photon loss limits their entanglement rate. Here we entangle a trapped 138Ba+ ion with a silicon-vacancy (SiV-) center in a diamond nanophotonic cavity. A photon emitted by the ion is converted in wavelength and encoding, reflected from the SiV-–cavity system and detected, so that a single detected photon heralds entanglement. Including all conversion losses, we generate ion–SiV- Bell pairs at an average rate of 1.03(1) kHz with a fidelity of 87.9(7)%. This is four times the rate of the fastest photonic link between two trapped ions and corresponds to one Bell pair per millisecond, matching the cycle time of planned trapped-ion processors.

Modular quantum computing offers a path to large-scale quantum systems by interconnecting smaller quantum processors [1, 2, 3, 4], analogous to the role of networking in modern datacenters. To implement fault-tolerant operations between modules, a modular quantum computer must be capable of consistently generating large numbers of high-fidelity entangled qubit pairs between modules. For known algorithms and plausible near-term qubit fidelities and quantum error correction schemes, estimates of the entanglement rate needed to support continuous logical operations between modules range from 10 to 100 kHz [5, 6, 7], at an infidelity about ten times higher than that of local two-qubit operations [8]. The fastest photonic link between trapped ions, which hold some of the highest reported local gate fidelities [9], produces 250 Bell pairs per second [10].

Photonically mediated entanglement offers a straightforward path to multiplexing and can be implemented using largely commercially available parts, but is also necessarily probabilistic [11]. The rate of photonic entanglement is a product of the attempt rate, the probability of a successful herald, and the number of multiplexed channels. For most atomic qubit systems, the attempt rate has a fixed upper limit set by the radiative lifetimes involved in state preparation [12, 10]. Therefore, most photonic entanglement architectures focus on increasing the number of channels [13] or the probability of successfully extracting a photon per channel [14].

Increasing the number of channels can be costly, because communication and computation then compete for the same resources, such as qubits, cooling and initialization [7]. Photon extraction efficiencies can be improved with larger numerical aperture (NA) optics for free-space emission [14], or by Purcell-enhancing qubit emission via cavities [15, 16]. The trade-off between NA and field of view makes it difficult to combine high-efficiency free-space collection with highly multiplexed schemes. Multiple imaging zones or cavities with Purcell enhancement offer a potential path around this. However, dielectric surfaces near the qubits degrade gate fidelities and coherence in both trapped-ion and neutral-atom systems [17, 18]. Optics therefore need to be placed farther from computational qubits, which requires either shuttling qubits to a communication zone [19, 20, 21] or long cavities, whose narrow linewidths slow the extraction of photons [22].

Better collection reduces photon loss but cannot remove it, so the heralding scheme sets how strongly the remaining loss limits the rate. In the two-photon schemes used for the fastest ion–ion links [12, 10], photons from both nodes must be detected, so the success probability scales with the square of the photon collection efficiency of a single node. Single-photon heralding between two emitters scales linearly, but it trades rate against fidelity through the excitation probability and requires interferometric phase stability and indistinguishable photons from the two nodes [23, 24, 25]. A quantum memory that reflects the photon emitted by the other node avoids these costs: a single detected photon heralds entanglement, the success probability scales linearly with the photon collection efficiency, the emitter can be excited with near-unit probability, and no two-photon interference is needed. Moreover, a reflective quantum memory can be entangled with any photon whose spectral width is smaller than the bandwidth of its spin-dependent reflection.

In this paper, we introduce a hybrid architecture that combines the free-space photon collection from an atomic qubit with the near-perfect efficiency from a solid-state memory in a cavity. We collect photons from ions via a conventional imaging system outside the vacuum chamber, without an optical cavity, reflect them from a qubit-cavity quantum memory system with high photon interaction efficiency, and detect them to produce a herald signal. Such heterogeneous links have been considered difficult because two different platforms must operate together through interfaces such as quantum frequency conversion. SiV- memories interact efficiently with photons but have been limited by the rate of their photon sources [26], whereas trapped ions emit photons at a high rate but collect them with low probability [10]. Entanglement between a trapped ion and a solid-state quantum memory was recently reported with a rare-earth ensemble memory [27]; here we use a single-spin memory and a single-photon herald, which together allow kilohertz rates.

The quantum memory is implemented as a silicon-vacancy center in a diamond nanophotonic cavity. SiV- centers in such cavities interact efficiently with photons [28], provide an electron–nuclear spin register in which a nuclear-controlled gate reaches 99.9% fidelity [9], and can be fabricated in large numbers on a single chip [30]. The memory is paired with an ion–photon interface in 138Ba+ [31], which has been used for the fastest ion–ion entanglement to date [10] and is compatible with leading ion quantum computing architectures [32, 33, 9]. Combining the two systems in a hybrid photonic entanglement scheme, we entangle the ion and the SiV- at a rate of 1.03 kHz, i.e. one entangled pair per millisecond on average, comparable to the computational cycle time of planned ion quantum computers [34].

A schematic of the experiment is illustrated in Figure 1(a,b). A single trapped 138Ba+ ion [1] is Doppler cooled and optically pumped into $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}=\ket{S_{1/2},m_{J}=+1/2}$ . Each ion–photon entanglement generation attempt starts with a picosecond $\sigma^{-}$ -polarized pulse at $493.5$ nm that excites the ion with near-unity probability to $\ket{P_{1/2},m_{J}=-1/2}$ , from which the ion spontaneously decays either to $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}=\ket{S_{1/2},m_{J}=-1/2}$ by emitting a $\pi$ -polarized photon or back to $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ by emitting a $\sigma^{-}$ -polarized photon, thereby entangling the ion’s electron spin with the photon polarization (decay to the $D_{3/2}$ manifold at 650 nm constitutes a loss channel and is repumped in the next attempt).

The entanglement is maximal only if the two decay channels contribute equally to the photon in the fiber. We collect the photon perpendicular to the quantization axis with an $\mathrm{NA}=0.75$ objective (see Supplemental Material (SM), Sec. S1). Coupling into a single-mode optical fiber maps $\sigma^{-}$ and $\pi$ emission onto orthogonal linear polarizations $H$ and $V$ , respectively [12]. The smaller branching probability of the $\pi$ transition is nearly compensated by its stronger transverse emission and higher fiber-coupling efficiency (see SM, Sec. S2). The resulting state is close to maximally entangled, $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}V_{493}}+\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}H_{493}}$ (normalization omitted throughout).

This polarization-encoded $493.5$ nm photon is not directly compatible with the SiV- memory, which requires a time-bin-encoded photon at $737.45$ nm [28, 26]. We therefore first convert the photon wavelength from $493.5$ nm to $737.45$ nm using polarization-insensitive quantum frequency conversion (QFC) in a Sagnac geometry (see SM, Sec. S3), $\ket{H_{493}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{QFC}}\ket{H_{737}}$ , $\ket{V_{493}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{QFC}}\ket{V_{737}}$ , and then convert the encoding with a basis converter (BC) consisting of an unbalanced Mach–Zehnder interferometer and a fast Pockels cell (see SM, Sec. S4), $\ket{V_{737}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{BC}}\ket{e}$ , $\ket{H_{737}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{BC}}\ket{l}$ , where $\ket{e}$ and $\ket{l}$ denote the early and late time bins that traverse the short and long arms of the interferometer, respectively. The ion–photon state entering the memory is thus $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}\ket{e}+\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}\ket{l}$ .

The ion–photon entanglement is transferred to the SiV- via a heralded spin–photon gate based on cavity-enhanced, spin-dependent reflection [10, 28, 26]. Owing to the strong coupling of the SiV- to the nanophotonic cavity at the operating frequency, an incident photon is reflected only if the SiV- electron spin is in $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ , whereas for $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ it is not reflected and lost. High-fidelity operation therefore requires the spectrum of the incident photon to lie within the bandwidth over which the cavity exhibits spin-dependent reflection. Before the photon arrives, the SiV- is prepared in an equal superposition of $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ and $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ , and a microwave $\pi$ pulse resonant with the SiV- electron transition is applied between the two photon time bins. The early bin is thus reflected only if the spin was initially in $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ (and is flipped to $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ by the $\pi$ pulse), and the late bin only if the spin was initially in $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ (and is flipped to $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ before the late bin arrives), so that, conditioned on reflection, the joint state becomes

$$ \ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}\ket{e}\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}+\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}\ket{l}\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}. $$

To herald the gate, the time-bin information must be erased by measuring the reflected photon in a superposition basis of $\ket{e}$ and $\ket{l}$ . For this purpose the reflected photon is sent back through the BC, where Faraday rotators separate the return path from the input and the Pockels cell now routes the early bin through the long arm and the late bin through the short arm. Both bins therefore acquire the same total delay and exit the BC simultaneously in a common spatial mode, with the time-bin qubit mapped back onto polarization, $\ket{e}\to\ket{H}$ , $\ket{l}\to\ket{V}$ . Since every photon traverses both arms exactly once, the interferometer phase cancels and no active stabilization of the BC is required. A projective measurement in the diagonal polarization basis, $\ket{D/A}=\ket{H}\pm\ket{V}$ , then erases the which-path information, and a detection event heralds the successful gate and projects the ion and the SiV- onto one of the two Bell states

$$ \ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}\pm\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}, $$

with the sign determined by which superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD) fires. Throughout, $\ket{0}$ ( $\ket{1}$ ) denotes the dark (bright) readout state of each qubit: for the ion $\ket{0}\equiv\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ (shelved) and $\ket{1}\equiv\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ ; for the SiV- $\ket{0}\equiv\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ and $\ket{1}\equiv\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ . We write two-qubit states as $\ket{\mathrm{ion},\mathrm{SiV}}$ . Spin flips that we apply to the SiV- before readout map the states of Eq. (2) onto the target Bell state $\ket{\Phi^{+}}=\ket{00}+\ket{11}$ , as described below.

To characterize the entanglement between the 138Ba+ ion and the SiV- memory, we perform tomography of the combined ion–SiV- state, which is summarized in Fig. 1(c). With a $1.1$ MHz attempt rate we obtain an entanglement rate of $R_{\mathrm{ent}}=1.032(11)$ kHz and $\mathcal{F}=87.9(7)\,\%$ .

The entanglement rate $R_{\mathrm{ent}}$ is a product of the attempt rate $f_{\mathrm{rep}}$ and the individual subsystem efficiencies: $\eta_{\mathrm{ion}}$ , $\eta_{\mathrm{sig}}$ , $\eta_{\mathrm{mem}}$ , and $\eta_{\mathrm{prot}}$ :

$$ R_{\mathrm{ent}}=f_{\mathrm{rep}}\;\eta_{\mathrm{ion}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{sig}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{mem}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{prot}}. $$

Multiplying the independently calibrated subsystem efficiencies (for definitions and values of $\eta_{i}$ see Table S3) predicts $R_{\mathrm{ent}}=1.21(20)$ kHz. The measured rate of $1.032(11)$ kHz lies $14\,\%$ below this prediction, within its uncertainty. We suspect that part of this difference arises from birefringence in the basis converter, which spatially separates the two polarization modes and thereby reduces the average fiber-coupling efficiency.

To identify what limits the fidelity, we combine independently calibrated error contributions of each subsystem (Table 1; SM, Table S4). The ion contributes most ( $\Delta\mathcal{F}=4.3\,\%$ ), mainly from optical-pumping light that leaks through the electro-optic modulators after a herald ( $\approx 1.6\,\%$ ) and from residual errors that we attribute to ion temperature and aberrations of the collection optics ( $\approx 1.5\,\%$ ). The memory contributes $3.9\,\%$ , about $3\,\%$ of which arises from the finite spin-dependent reflection contrast of the cavity-coupled SiV- and from nuclear-spin flips during the sequence, while microwave pulse errors and residual dephasing under XY8 decoupling each remain below $0.4\,\%$ . Frequency conversion contributes $2.9\,\%$ , almost entirely through conversion noise that produces false heralds. Photons that reach the memory but are lost before detection dephase the SiV- and contribute $1.9\,\%$ ; because this error accumulates over the attempts in a batch, it sets the rate–fidelity trade-off in Fig. 2(d). Together, these contributions predict $\mathcal{F}=87.4\,\%$ with $\langle XX\rangle=0.81$ and $\langle ZZ\rangle=0.87$ , in agreement with the tomographically reconstructed state ( $\mathcal{F}=87.9(7)\,\%$ ). None of the dominant errors is fundamental: narrower spectral filtering of the conversion noise, higher EOM extinction, higher cavity–SiV- contrast and a higher return efficiency from the memory to the detectors would each directly reduce the infidelity.

We implement the experimental sequence with a commercial modular control system. Its FPGA-based sequencer executes the pulse sequences and can branch in real time. Figure 2(a, b) shows a control-flow diagram of the sequence (see SM, Sec. S8 for additional details).

The delivery of each entangled state starts with an initialization step. It consists of Doppler cooling of the ion, initialization of the SiV- nuclear spin, and preparation of the SiV- electron spin in a balanced superposition state. We then start a batch of up to $15$ entanglement attempts. Each attempt consists of ion repumping, pulsed excitation of the ion to emit a photon, polarization switching with the Pockels cell, a microwave $\pi$ pulse that flips the SiV- spin between the two time bins, and detection and time-tagging of the photon. The microwave $\pi$ pulses alternate between the $X$ and $Y$ axes according to the XY8 sequence, which preserves the SiV- coherence better than pulses about a single axis. If a photon is detected in the $48$ ns detection window, which spans the photon wave packet (SM, Sec. S8), the sequence exits the batch and starts the readout step. If no attempt in the batch succeeds, we apply a reset step, which consists of Doppler cooling of the ion and preparation of the SiV- electron spin in a balanced superposition state. We then start a new batch of entanglement attempts.

During the readout step, we apply two real-time corrections (SM, Sec. S8 and Fig. S2): a phase correction on the ion compensates for the variable photon emission time, and a correction on the SiV- compensates for which detector clicked and for the SiV- phase at the photon interaction. We merge the latter with the remaining pulses of the XY8 sequence, whose number depends on how many attempts preceded the herald. Completing the sequence, with an extra $\pi$ pulse when needed, returns the SiV- spin to its initial frame, which interchanges $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ and $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}$ in Eq. (2). The delivered state is therefore $\ket{\Phi^{+}}=\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}\downarrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}+\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}\uparrow_{\mathrm{SiV}}}=\ket{00}+\ket{11}$ . These corrections could also be applied after the measurement, by relabeling the outcomes according to which detector clicked and when. Applying them in real time makes every herald deliver the same state $\ket{\Phi^{+}}$ , which is required when the entangled pair is used as a resource, as in distributed quantum computing.

Finally, we measure the two qubits in the selected bases: for every heralded event, the control system applies the basis rotations for the current measurement setting, together with the real-time corrections described above. For full state tomography, we use the $9$ measurement settings $\{X,Y,Z\}_{\text{ion}}\otimes\{X,Y,Z\}_{\text{SiV${}^{-}${}}}$ . From these, we calculate the two-qubit correlators $\braket{ij}\equiv\braket{\sigma_{i}\otimes\sigma_{j}}_{\rho}=\text{Tr}(\rho~\sigma_{i}\otimes\sigma_{j})$ (see SM, Sec. S7). We then reconstruct the density matrix of the generated entangled state using maximum likelihood estimation, and bootstrapping for error bars on the fidelity. Occasionally, the ion is lost from the trap or the SiV- changes charge state. Both failures cause an abrupt and complete loss of signal. In these cases we stop the acquisition, restore the system, and discard the full interrupted dataset. This decision depends only on the presence of the ion and of the SiV- readout signal, never on the measured correlations.

We measure the time needed to generate the entangled state from the beginning of the initialization step to the beginning of the readout step using the FPGA on-board clock ( $4$ ns resolution), obtaining a mean time to success of $969(10)$ µs, and a mean number of attempts of $731(8)$ (see Fig. 2(c)). This interval excludes the readout step ( $664$ µs per event), which characterizes the state and is not optimized for speed; in a distributed quantum computer, gates that consume the pair would take its place. Including the readout step, the wall-clock rate of generated and measured pairs is $612(4)$ Hz. By increasing the number of attempts per batch, we can reduce the relative overhead that the initialization and reset steps have on the time to success, therefore increasing the overall rate (see Fig. 2(d)). This comes at the expense of a reduced entangled state fidelity: the leading source of error is the increased chance per batch that a photon from the ion reaches the quantum memory but gets lost on the way back and is not detected, therefore dephasing the SiV- which will not be in the correct state for the next attempt (see SM, Sec. S5). This effect can be mitigated with increased detector efficiencies and reduced return loss from the nanophotonic cavity and the basis converter, and by collecting and heralding on photons transmitted through the cavity, in addition to reflected photons. Several pre-initialized memories addressed in turn would also allow each memory to be reset after a few attempts without pausing the ion.

Discussion. We have established an entangled link between a trapped-ion qubit and an efficient quantum memory with a fidelity of $87.9(7)\,\%$ at a rate comparable to local operations between ions, a step toward the 10–100 kHz rates required for distributed quantum computation. On the ion side, the link needs no cavity and no optics inside the vacuum chamber: an objective outside the vacuum window collects the photons and couples them into a single-mode fiber.

The dilution refrigerator used here is not a fundamental requirement either: strained SiV- centers have been operated at temperatures up to $1.5$ K [9], which compact closed-cycle cryostats can reach. Furthermore, the memory provides the operations needed for a network layer [37] that distributes entanglement between processors: the 29Si nuclear spin of the SiV- can store entanglement while new links are generated [9], SiV- nodes have performed Bell-state measurements on multiple photons [28], and two SiV- nodes have been entangled over deployed fiber [26]. All stages of the link (frequency conversion, basis conversion and the memory) are compatible with integrated photonics [30, 38], which would reduce loss and improve stability. We expect that a higher ion-to-fiber coupling, a more efficient signal chain, and replacing the amplitude-based spin–photon gate of the SiV- by a phase gate, which reflects the photon in both spin states and therefore works with strongly overcoupled cavities [39], will raise the entanglement rate to $>5$ kHz.

These abilities can be combined to produce ion-ion entanglement between quantum processors for extended error-corrected circuits, providing a scaling route for quantum computers [40]. In addition, because SiVs interact efficiently with a range of photons, they can serve as a photonic front-end that receives photons for ion processors. For example, they can receive sparse photons from a weak optical sensing target and teleport the photon state into an ion processor for algorithms such as quantum principal component analysis (PCA) [41, 42]. Similarly, SiVs can receive weak photonic signals over fiber in quantum communication or blind quantum computing [43] and pass the resulting states to ion processors for error correction. We expect this heterogeneous system to benefit applications that combine low-loss interaction with photons and quantum processing.

## S1 Ion trap, qubit control and photon collection

### Ion trap and qubit control

The 138Ba+ ion is trapped in a four-rod Paul trap with a design similar to that of Ref. [1]. The ion trap is wider along one dimension to maximize the numerical aperture for light collection ( $\mathrm{NA}=0.75$ , Sec. S2). The ion secular frequencies along the three principal axes are $(0.57,\,0.72,\,1.07)$ MHz. We use two rings of permanent magnets and shim coils to apply a magnetic field of 3.68 G at the ion. This gives a ground-state Zeeman qubit splitting of $\omega_{\mathrm{ion}}=2\pi\times 10.30\,\mathrm{MHz}$ .

At the beginning of each entanglement sequence, we Doppler cool the ion for $20\,\mu$ s. We then execute repeated entanglement attempts, with a $3.1\,\mu$ s recooling period after every batch of one lead-in and up to $8N-1$ attempts, as shown in Fig. 2(a). Before each excitation pulse, we prepare the ion in $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}=\ket{S_{1/2},m_{J}=+1/2}$ by optical pumping with the $493.5$ nm $\sigma^{+}$ beam for 160 ns. To repump the ion out of the $D_{3/2}$ manifold, we turn on the 650 nm beam 160 ns before the $493.5$ nm optical-pumping light and keep it on for 320 ns. With this pumping duration, the measured probability of preparing the ion in $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ is $0.82(2)$ (Table S3). Incomplete pumping leaves residual population dark to the excitation pulse, so, when false heralds are rare, it primarily reduces the success probability per attempt rather than the heralded-state fidelity. We therefore optimize the pumping duration to maximize the overall entanglement-generation rate, accepting imperfect preparation in exchange for more attempts per second.

We detect the ion state by shelving $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ in $\ket{D}=\ket{D_{5/2},m_{J}=+3/2}$ with a narrow-linewidth ( $<1\,$ kHz) 1762 nm laser. The $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ state fluoresces under $493.5$ nm and 650 nm illumination, while the shelved population remains dark. We assign the dark state ( $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ ) to $\ket{0}$ and the bright state ( $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ ) to $\ket{1}$ . We apply the fluorescence beams for $500\,\mu$ s and detect the scattered photons with a Hamamatsu ORCA-Quest 2 camera. A histogram of the detected photoelectron counts is shown in Fig. S1. The measured detection fidelity is $0.9935(6)$ for the shelved state and $0.9993(2)$ for the bright state, and most of the error is caused by incomplete 1762 nm transfer to $\ket{D}$ . For some diagnostic measurements, we reduce this error with a second shelving pulse. After the first 1762 nm pulse transfers $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ to $\ket{D}$ , a second 1762 nm pulse shelves the residual $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ population to $\ket{D_{5/2},m_{J}=-3/2}$ . This double shelving squares the shelving failure probability and makes the dark-state readout error negligible.

We also use the 1762 nm laser for coherent operations between the qubit states. We first convert the ground-state qubit to an optical qubit by shelving $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ in $\ket{D}$ . A $\pi/2$ pulse with variable phase $\phi_{1762}$ then couples $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ and $\ket{D}$ for single-qubit operations. After photon emission, the ion accrues a phase $\phi=\omega_{\text{ion}}\,\Delta t$ , where $\Delta t$ is the time since emission. Because $\Delta t$ changes from shot to shot, the phase also changes. For each herald, the controller reads the photon time tag and adds a compensating phase to $\phi_{1762}$ in real time (Fig. S2).

We switch most laser beams with double-pass AOMs. To reduce the turn-on latency, we pass the $493.5$ nm $\sigma^{+}$ optical-pumping light through two Mach–Zehnder (MZ) EOMs in series. The MZ EOM paths have turn-on latencies below 100 ns and sub-nanosecond rise times. We condition the $493.5$ nm MZ EOM pulses on whether a photon is detected during the current attempt (Fig. S15). The AOM paths have latencies greater than 500 ns, so we cannot turn them off in time after a photon detection. Thus, after a herald, the suppression of the $493.5$ nm optical-pumping light depends only on the combined extinction of the two MZ EOMs ( $\sim$ 47 dB). Leakage light incident on the ion after a herald can optically pump the ion and thereby degrade the heralded ion–photon state. From ion–photon measurements at $493.5$ nm with and without pre-triggering the AOMs, we find that this leakage flips the measured correlation with probability $0.009$ in $XX$ and $0.015$ in $ZZ$ (see below and Table S4).

### Pulsed excitation and ion–photon entanglement

A mode-locked Ti:sapphire laser (Spectra-Physics Tsunami) at 987 nm generates 10 ps pulses at a 79.3 MHz repetition rate. An externally triggered pulse-picker selects pulses from this train. We adjust the pulse-picker timing to transmit the selected pulse and suppress the neighboring pulses. Since the attempt rate is not commensurate with the repetition rate of the pulsed laser, the selected pulse arrives at a random time within a 12.6 ns interval. This results in a photon emission shape where the exponential decay of the excited state is convolved with a uniform distribution of 12.6 ns width (Fig. S2). We frequency-double the selected pulses in a periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) waveguide (NTT Innovative Devices Corporation) to generate $493.5$ nm excitation light. An AOM gates this light before delivery to the ion. We time the falling edge of the AOM gate to suppress subsequent pulses. We calibrate the pulse energy by scanning the AOM RF amplitude and set it to maximize the excitation probability. Conditional on preparation in $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ , the excitation probability per selected pulse is $0.97(2)$ (Fig. S3).

After excitation, the ion decays to $S_{1/2}$ with a probability of $\approx 0.73$ [2], summed over the two useful Zeeman decay channels. Decay to $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}=\ket{S_{1/2},m_{J}=-1/2}$ emits a $\pi$ -polarized photon, and decay back to $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ emits a $\sigma^{-}$ -polarized photon. The Clebsch–Gordan coefficients give total emission probabilities of $2/3$ for $\sigma^{-}$ and $1/3$ for $\pi$ . Perpendicular to the quantization axis, the $\pi$ emission is twice as strong as the $\sigma^{-}$ emission, so the two components have equal amplitudes along the collection axis. Over the full $\mathrm{NA}=0.75$ aperture, the collected light contains fewer $\pi$ than $\sigma^{-}$ photons (43:57), but the lower fiber-coupling efficiency for $\sigma^{-}$ light compensates this difference (Sec. S2). The single-mode fiber maps $\sigma^{-}$ and $\pi$ onto $H_{493}$ and $V_{493}$ , which gives the ion–photon state $\ket{\downarrow_{\mathrm{ion}}V_{493}}+\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}H_{493}}$ .

We characterize the ion–photon state via joint measurements of the ion’s internal state and the photon’s polarization. To this end, the photons are directed to a polarization analyzer at 493 nm, consisting of a quarter-wave plate, a half-wave plate, and a polarizing beam splitter (PBS), with a single-photon counting module (SPCM) at each PBS output port. We rotate the photon-analysis waveplates to measure the polarization correlations. We also scan the phase of the 1762 nm ion-analysis pulse to probe the coherence between the two components of the entangled state. Figure S4 shows the resulting correlations and coherence measurements. From the measured correlations $\langle ZZ\rangle=0.949(6)$ and $\langle XX\rangle=0.939(6)$ , we obtain a lower bound on the ion–photon Bell-state fidelity of $F\geq(\langle ZZ\rangle+\langle XX\rangle)/2=0.944(4)$ , without correction for state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors. To test the rest of the QFC and BC apparatus, we shift the converted light frequency and use the cavity as a bare reflector. For photons converted to $737.45$ nm and reflected off-resonantly from the cavity (Fig. S5), we measure $\langle ZZ\rangle=0.923(7)$ and $\langle XX\rangle=0.935(7)$ , giving $F\geq 0.929(5)$ without SPAM correction.

The ion contributions to the combined ion–SiV- error budget are listed in Table S4. Each entry is the probability that an error flips the measured correlation in the given basis, and we assume equal errors for $XX$ and $YY$ . Together, the ion entries reproduce the measured ion– $493.5$ nm photon correlators $\langle XX\rangle=0.939(6)$ and $\langle ZZ\rangle=0.949(6)$ .

The largest ion error comes from optical-pumping light that reaches the ion after a herald. The AOMs cannot switch off in time, so after a herald only the two MZ EOMs suppress the pre-triggered 493.5 nm pumping light. To quantify this error, we compare the above with measurements without AOM pre-triggers (by modifying the experimental sequence, which then runs at roughly half the repetition rate; Fig. S6), which give $\langle ZZ\rangle=0.984(5)$ and $\langle XX\rangle=0.956(5)$ . We obtain the leakage error probability in each basis by comparing the correlators measured with and without AOM pre-triggers, which differ only in whether pumping light can reach the ion after a herald. The $ZZ$ measurement without pre-triggers uses double shelving: after the first 1762 nm pulse transfers $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ to $\ket{D}$ , a second 1762 nm pulse shelves the residual $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ population to $\ket{D_{5/2},m_{J}=-3/2}$ . This makes the dark-state readout error negligible, which we account for in the comparison, giving leakage error probabilities of $0.009$ in $XX$ and $0.015$ in $ZZ$ .

Each ion readout error flips the measured correlation. The shelved state reads bright with probability $0.0065$ and the bright state reads dark with probability $0.0007$ (Fig. S1). Because the entangled state has equal populations in the two ion states, the ion state detection gives an error probability of $(0.0065+0.0007)/2\approx 0.004$ in each basis.

Photons detected in the first $\approx 10$ ns of the detection window herald a lower-fidelity state: post-selecting on arrival times $t>10$ ns (73% of events) increases $\langle XX\rangle$ from $0.956(5)$ to $0.967(6)$ , while $\langle ZZ\rangle$ changes only from $0.984(5)$ to $0.987(5)$ . For excitations early in the pulse-picker cycle, the AOM gate is still open when the next laser pulse arrives, and this residual pulse can re-excite the ion. Re-excitation removes the coherence of the entangled state but changes the $ZZ$ correlation only in the $\ket{\uparrow_{\mathrm{ion}}}$ branch, which gives error probabilities of $0.006$ in $XX$ and $0.002$ in $ZZ$ . Background counts, amplitude imbalance of the collected state, time-tag quantization, magnetic-field dephasing and polarization mixing in the collection optics each contribute less than $0.002$ . We attribute the remaining error to ion temperature during fast-loop attempts and residual aberrations of the collection optics.

## S2 Microscope design

The microscope assembly comprises two objectives built by Special Optics. The first, with 0.75 NA, collects 16.9% of the light emitted by the ion and collimates it. Special Optics reports a single-pass wavefront error of $0.068\lambda$ rms at $493.5$ nm, primarily spherical aberration. The objective is compensated for a 4 mm SF57 glass vacuum window. All the glass up to the fiber is SF57, chosen for its extremely low stress-optic coefficient of $2\cdot 10^{-8}\text{ mm}^{2}/\text{N}$ [3]. This mitigates ion-photon entanglement infidelities: inhomogeneous stress in the glass can imprint different polarizations on photons passing through different parts of the large-aperture assembly, contaminating the state. The first objective maximizes numerical aperture within the space set by the re-entrant viewport used for optical access. The second must mode-match the focused beam to the fiber mode to maximize coupling efficiency. To find its optimal numerical aperture, we computed the vectorial electric field the microscope projects onto the fiber [4]. A simpler scalar method, which assumes the objective Fourier-transforms the collimated field, gives the same optimal NA and is relatively independent of apodization factors. Only the vectorial method, however, captures the differential fiber coupling efficiency: 78% for $\pi$ light and 57% for $\sigma$ light due to the orbital angular momentum the photon acquires on emission. The higher fiber-coupling efficiency for $\pi$ light compensates the residual imbalance of the collected $\pi$ and $\sigma$ components (43:57 at NA = 0.75), such that the fiber-coupled state is balanced to within 2% (51:49), corresponding to a fidelity with the maximally entangled state above 99.9% [4]. The transmission from the ion to the fiber facet, through the collection objective, the vacuum window and the focusing objective, is $85(3)\,\%$ (Table S3). This is limited mainly by residual reflections at the many anti-reflection-coated surfaces of the multi-element objectives. We achieve 40% fiber coupling (Table S3). The Zemax model provided by the manufacturer shows that the objective is not diffraction-limited: 55% of the light falls in the central lobe of the Airy disk, as opposed to the 84% expected for a diffraction-limited beam. Including these aberrations, our scalar model finds 52% fiber coupling efficiency for a centered beam, i.e. for $\pi$ light with the aligned objective, instead of the 78% above. This is, to our knowledge, the main reason why we do not obtain higher fiber coupling. We numerically ruled out excessive ion temperature as a significant contribution.

### Mode of the S405-XP fiber and its free-space expansion

Estimating fiber coupling requires precise knowledge of the fiber core mode shape. Using the manufacturer’s parameters [5] for the core radius $a=1.5\,\mu$ m and numerical aperture $\sqrt{n_{\text{core}}^{2}-n_{\text{cladding}}^{2}}=0.12$ , we solve the equations of Ref. [6] to derive the shape of the LP ${}_{01}(r)$ single mode. This mode is well approximated by a Gaussian $E_{0}\exp(-r^{2}/w_{0}^{2})$ . The overlap between the two exceeds 99% but the modes are not strictly interchangeable. Outside the core, the LP01 decays as the Bessel function $K_{0}(\alpha r)\sim\exp(-\alpha r)/\sqrt{\alpha r}$ , where $\alpha$ is a numerical constant. It therefore does not propagate as a Gaussian beam and expands significantly more slowly. Figure S7 shows how the LP01 mode (solid blue) and its best-matched Gaussian (dashed red), both starting with a waist radius $w_{0}=1.7\,\mu$ m, expand at different rates. The manufacturer’s data indicates a mode field diameter (MFD $=2w_{0}$ ) of 3.3 $\mu$ m at 405 nm and 4.6 $\mu$ m at 630 nm. A simple linear scaling would give $w_{0}=1.9\,\mu$ m at $493.5$ nm. Such a Gaussian beam (dotted red) matches the LP01 well at long distances. However, at the facet, the mode is best matched by a Gaussian of 1.7 $\mu$ m, not 1.9 $\mu$ m. We experimentally measured the beam profile and found a far-field size smaller than either prediction, which indicates that the mode field radius is likely greater than 1.7 $\mu$ m. We confirmed this on two different fibers. For simplicity, we used the calculated LP01 to compute the mode overlap with the ion field and found the optimal NA for the focusing microscope to be $\approx 0.10$ .

## S3 Polarization-insensitive frequency conversion

We convert single photons at $493.5$ nm from 138Ba+ to the emission band of silicon-vacancy (SiV) centers in diamond near $737.45$ nm by difference-frequency generation (DFG) with a continuous-wave pump near $1492.3$ nm in a temperature-stabilized periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) ridge waveguide (NTT Innovative Devices Corporation; 22 mm long, $11.3\times 11.6\,\mu$ m cross section, poling period $\Lambda=5.9\,\mu$ m). Because DFG in PPLN acts on only one polarization, the waveguide sits in a Sagnac loop, in which the two polarization components are converted in counter-propagating directions and recombined with intrinsic phase stability, preserving the polarization state of the photon [7, 8]. We refer to this scheme as polarization-insensitive quantum frequency conversion (QFC). Signal photons and pump are split by a tri-color polarizing beam splitter (PBS) into the two arms of the loop, and a dual-wavelength half-wave plate (HWP) inside the loop aligns the polarization of both counter-propagating beams with the PPLN crystal axis. Waveplates before the loop set the relative pump power in the clockwise (CW) and anticlockwise (ACW) arms, balancing the H and V conversion efficiencies.

The wavelengths are fixed by four requirements: the input must match the $493.5$ nm Ba+ transition; the output must reach $737.45$ nm with 200–300 GHz of tunability to cover the inhomogeneous distribution of strained SiV- transition frequencies; the pump must be the longest of the three wavelengths, so that noise from spontaneous Raman scattering and spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) of the pump falls at frequencies below the signal band; and the pump linewidth must be well below the $\sim$ 20 MHz signal linewidth to preserve the photon’s spectral and temporal shape. Reaching near-unity conversion also requires 200–300 mW of pump power coupled into the fundamental waveguide mode. We use a single-frequency diode laser (Toptica DL pro) amplified to 5 W by a Raman fiber amplifier (MPB Communications; 2 nm bandwidth at $1492.3$ nm). A software lock to a wavemeter (HighFinesse WS6-200) provides tuning and suppresses long-term drift, while a 200 MHz acousto-optic modulator allows for fast in-sequence switching of converted signal light and pump noise. The setup spans three fiber-linked breadboards—pump, Sagnac loop, and basis conversion—to minimize distance and latency from the ion.

### Efficiency

*Figure S8: External conversion efficiency of the QFC as a function of transmitted pump power for the clockwise (CW) and anticlockwise (ACW) arms of the Sagnac loop.*

The fiber-to-fiber conversion efficiency is 47.5%, measured from the converter input fiber to the free-space exit of the filtering stage. It is limited by transmission to the chip input facets (92%), waveguide coupling ( $>$ 90%), internal transmission at $493.5$ nm ( $>$ 95%), internal conversion efficiency ( $>$ 90%), output fiber coupling ( $>$ 80%), and spectral filtering (88%). Light is coupled into and out of the waveguide with $f=11$ mm aspheric lenses on three-axis stages (Newport 562-XYZ). Chromatic aberration of the lenses forces a trade-off between pump and signal coupling, so the pump coupling reaches only $\sim$ 75%, and residual astigmatism limits the output coupling. Internal conversion reaches 92–94% when well aligned. The Sagnac board alone reaches 57% input-to-output efficiency, with a small asymmetry between arms (Fig. S8) attributable to the angled chip facets and to chromatic dispersion of the three beams, which prevents simultaneous optimization of both arms. With an efficiency imbalance of 1–2 % between the two arms of the Sagnac loop, the polarization-dependent conversion efficiency reduces the fidelity by $\lesssim 10^{-4}$ , so the 0.10 % entry in Table S4 is an upper bound.

### Noise and spectral filtering

Two noise sources limit the signal-to-noise ratio. First, second-harmonic generation (SHG) of the pump produces roughly 1 $\mu$ W near 746 nm; although this process is poorly phase matched, the high pump intensity makes it significant. Because SHG depends on the poling period and temperature, we survey the 12 waveguides on the chip once the target SiV- frequency is chosen and select the one whose DFG phase-matching temperature yields the least SHG. Two angle-tuned 200 GHz etalon filters (custom, Thorlabs) in series, with transmissions of 96 % and 92 % (88 % combined, Table S3), then remove the residual 746 nm light. Because their transmission is sensitive to beam collimation, they are placed in the collimated section of the basis converter. Second, a broadband noise pedestal falls directly in the $737.45$ nm signal band. We attribute it to three potential sources: SHG of the Raman fiber amplifier’s noise pedestal, noise accumulated in the long pump delivery fiber, and amplified spontaneous emission near $737.45$ nm. A 12 nm bandpass filter on the pump removes $>95\%$ of these counts. We characterize the effective SNR of the QFC by running the main experiment sequence with the light from the ion blocked. Comparing the herald click rate in this case versus the case in which the ion light is unblocked, we estimate an SNR of 27.

## S4 Polarization to time-bin conversion and circulation

The basis conversion is a two-stage process. First, we use an unbalanced Mach–Zehnder interferometer with a polarizing beam splitter (PBS) both at the input and output as a time-delay interferometer (TDI). The input PBS splits the incoming polarization qubit into its $V$ and $H$ components and routes them into the short and long arms of the TDI, respectively ( $V\to e$ , $H\to l$ ). This way, we induce a time delay between the two polarization components before recombining them into the same spatial mode at the output PBS. The induced time delay is set by the path length difference between the arms of the interferometer. We induce a delay of 72 ns using a delay fiber of $\approx 15$ m length. The minimum time delay is given by the temporal duration of the photon ( $\tau_{\mathrm{ph}}=48$ ns) and the duration of the $\pi$ -pulse ( $\tau_{\pi}=18$ ns) applied to the electron spin of the SiV-.

As the cavity only supports a single linear polarization mode, the polarization of both time bins must be matched to this state. However, after the output PBS of the TDI, both time bins are orthogonally polarized. Therefore, in the second stage of the conversion process, we rotate the polarization of the late time bin (which traversed the long arm) to match that of the early time bin using a Pockels cell. To reduce the effect of spatially inhomogeneous birefringence of the Pockels cell, we reduce the beam size in the Pockels cell by installing a telescope with a magnification of $M=1/2$ in front of it and $M=2$ behind it, each consisting of two spherical singlets with focal lengths of $f=100$ mm and $f=200$ mm. After the Pockels cell, the photon is coupled into a single-mode fiber connecting the basis converter to the SiV-–cavity system.

Overall, this conversion yields the map

$$ \alpha\ket{H}+\beta\ket{V}\;\rightarrow\;\tilde{\alpha}\ket{l}+\tilde{\beta}\ket{e}, $$

with $\alpha,\beta,\tilde{\alpha},\tilde{\beta}$ being complex probability amplitudes ( $|\alpha|^{2}+|\beta|^{2}=|\tilde{\alpha}|^{2}+|\tilde{\beta}|^{2}=1$ ). As the long and short arms differ in efficiency, mainly because of the fiber coupling in the long arm, the amplitudes of the output qubit are unbalanced relative to the input qubit. However, this rotation is compensated after reflection from the SiV-–cavity system, as the photon passes again through the basis converter in the opposite direction and each polarization component now traverses the other arm. On the return path, the conversion is reversed and the time-bin qubit is mapped back onto a polarization qubit. To erase the time-bin information, the Pockels cell is used to set the polarization such that the early (late) time bin is routed through the long (short) arm, so that both polarization components arrive simultaneously at the input PBS. To route the photon at the input PBS to the polarization-resolving detection setup instead of back to the quantum frequency conversion setup, each arm of the TDI includes a Faraday rotator and a set of waveplates, which together function analogously to an optical circulator. A Faraday rotator induces a non-reciprocal $45^{\circ}$ rotation of linearly polarized light, which in combination with the waveplates gives a propagation-direction-dependent polarization rotation, e.g., in the short arm mapping $V$ onto $V$ for the forward pass vs. $V$ onto $H$ for the backward pass.

Using the basis converter in double-pass configuration comes with two major advantages. First, it eliminates the need for active phase stabilization, as both time bins accumulate the same total phase along their passage through both the long and short arm, provided the interferometer phase is stable on the timescale of the round trip (which is $\approx 300$ ns). Second, the arm-dependent (i.e., polarization-dependent) loss is balanced on the second passage and therefore does not affect the fidelity, only the efficiency.

The overall single-pass efficiency of the basis converter is $59(2)\%$ . To measure the basis converter efficiency, we inject pulses at the single-photon level, detuned from the cavity resonance, into the basis converter. To calibrate the input photon flux, we use a flip mirror directly at the input of the basis converter. The light reflected off the flip mirror is coupled into an optical fiber and sent onto a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD).

Without the flip mirror in the optical path, the pulses pass through the basis converter, are reflected off the cavity and back-propagate through the basis converter before eventually being detected by the SNSPDs of the polarization-resolving detection setup. The ratio of detected counts on these SNSPDs and the detected counts at the input of the basis converter gives us a round-trip efficiency and allows us to calculate the single-pass efficiency. The single-pass efficiency does not include the detection efficiencies of the SNSPDs, the transmission through the fiber to the cavity (back and forth), or the reflection coefficient of the cavity, which are characterized separately. ## S5 Diamond nanophotonic SiV memory

### Setup: dilution refrigerator, readout optics, and MW/RF drive electronics

*Figure S9: Diagram of the quantum memory apparatus. Excitation sources are combined with a 50:50 fiber beamsplitter and coupled into the dilution refrigerator via a 99:1 fiber beamsplitter. The fiber is tapered and coupled to the device at the base of the dilution refrigerator. Reflected photons are detected by SNSPDs after passing through the basis converter.
